title: Maybe Donald Trump Doesn’t Want His Party to Win the Midterms
summary: I put it to you plainly: Would someone who wanted to win the midterms be behaving as Donald Trump has?We are a full 20 minutes into Trump’s address to the nation, on the day before Election Day, and he has yet to pivot from pipes. He is standing beside, of all things, the Reflecting Pool, and he is ...
content:
I put it to you plainly: Would someone who wanted to win the midterms be behaving as Donald Trump has?

We are a full 20 minutes into Trump’s address to the nation, on the day before Election Day, and he has yet to pivot from pipes. He is standing beside, of all things, the Reflecting Pool, and he is talking about, of all things, the pipes. With visual aids, prepared in advance, lest anyone say “Surely this was some mistake!” (It was some mistake, but, like so many Trump-era mistakes, it was a mistake that had been planned.) He is reflecting on the lifespan of grass. (“Like the human being, grass has a life also.”) Will someone tell him that something big is happening in the country tomorrow?

Here he stands, for his closing remarks to the American people. And those closing remarks are overwhelmingly about the Reflecting Pool. As he speaks, he holds up his slides, each of which he describes with the beleaguered energy of an old laptop with too many open tabs. He goes on about the vandals with box cutters and knives (there were no vandals with box cutters and knives) who attacked the pool.

Look, if I wanted to win the midterms, and I were Donald Trump, I would not go stand in front of the physical symbol of my failure and remind people that my chosen team installed its lining so badly that it looked like the work of vandals with box cutters, but that is just me. I am not Donald Trump for numerous reasons. I enjoy hugging my family and often admit that I was wrong. I am not Narcissus-levels of obsessed with a reflective body of water.

If I had been as embroiled in an unsuccessful pool renovation as Donald Trump has, you could not drag me to the pool with wild horses, not even next to a nifty little prepared sign with a picture of the pool that reads: Back, and more beautiful than ever! Maybe he is trying to spin the “blue wave” as something positive that he has done to remove algae from the Reflecting Pool? I could not tell you. Maybe he thinks that if he can just clean the pool enough, everyone will look into it and see the reflection that he sees?

If I were Donald Trump and I wanted to win the midterms, I wouldn’t march from state to state demanding to be remembered. This is like if the albatross around your neck thought it was helping.

The best that can be said of his Reflecting Pool speech is that it included no odes to anyone’s posterior, not that of Jon Husted or Nicki Minaj or even Abraham Lincoln, who might have sprung to mind because he was seated so near. And that there was only one joke about renaming the reflecting pool the Trump Reflecting Pool (which was a joke, I think).

Of course, I do not want to imply that the speech lacked any of the president’s usual transphobic, bigoted scaremongering about “mutilization” and “jihadists.” Those were also there. But I am not sure that someone standing in front of the worst metaphor for his presidency and sleepily saying that “communist jihadists” (how does this combination of beliefs work, exactly, in his mind?) are coming to take the Senate is the winning closer he pictured. Nor is his announcement that a deal with Iran “could happen.” (Anything could happen!) Or his bewildering statement that the “Green New Scam” predicted that we would all be dead in 12 years? “Here we are, we’re not dead.” Got it. Clear as the … now-at-least-temporarily-algae-free pool surface!

If I were Donald Trump and I wanted to win the midterms, I would certainly not go stand in front of the Reflecting Pool and say any of this. Maybe, instead, I would go hide in a deep hole and hope that no one remembered I existed or noticed anything I had done. But I guess it is too late for that.

title: Trump’s Venezuela Project Just Got a Lot More Complicated
summary: Two days after María Corina Machado’s high-stakes return to Venezuela last week, she walked into her low-slung party headquarters, which had been raided and vandalized by supporters of the regime that had forced her into exile. The graffiti had been painted over and the debris had been cleared. Mach...
content:
Two days after María Corina Machado’s high-stakes return to Venezuela last week, she walked into her low-slung party headquarters, which had been raided and vandalized by supporters of the regime that had forced her into exile. The graffiti had been painted over and the debris had been cleared. Machado was there for her first major meeting back in Caracas, with about 100 family members of political prisoners. Machado could see that many held photos of their detained relatives. Many also wore shirts that read Libertad.

“They persecute the innocent using all the power of the state,” Machado said in a speech. She didn’t mention names, but everyone in the crowd knew that she was referring to the cadre of leaders now running the country under U.S. tutelage. Still being held were at least 400 political prisoners, according to civil-society groups, people Machado referred to as “our absolute priority” and “our heroes.”

Eglis Manaure was in the small crowd, holding a photo of her husband, Enrique Nauris Parada, one of the 400. He had been detained since 2020. Listening to Machado speak, Manaure thought not only of the prospect that her husband might finally be freed, but also that his jailers might soon be punished. “Whatever form of justice she”—meaning Machado—“decides,” Manaure told us after the meeting. In the days following her return, Machado has begun talking about justice, reparations, and the “dismantling of the repressive state.” Put another way: One U.S. ally in Venezuela appears to be calling for the prosecution of another. It is an early glimpse into the rivalry the United States will now have to manage as it oversees Venezuela’s democratic transition. For 10 months, ever since what President Trump described today as the “conquest of Venezuela,” the administration has consolidated power around a single pliant figure: Interim President Delcy Rodríguez. Through Rodríguez, the U.S. was able to negotiate an opaque petroleum agreement that Trump, in a dubious claim, has called “the biggest oil deal in world history.” (Trump, in another dubious claim, said today that “we’re taking in hundreds of billions of dollars of oil.”) In a January interview with The Atlantic, he said of Rodríguez: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price.”

But as of last week, the U.S. is no longer ruling over a unipolar Venezuela. Machado is by far the most popular figure in Venezuelan politics. In recent days, her supporters have crowded highways and plazas and churches across parts of the country to get a look at the returned leader. People have wept in the streets. Last Tuesday, while Machado met with the families of political prisoners, Rodríguez held her own rally, where she danced on a stage to popular songs—a stunt that was widely mocked by Venezuelans. And yet it was Rodríguez, watching her power come under threat, who derided Machado’s return as a “show.”

In its first 10 months running Venezuela, the Trump administration chose to work with vestiges of Nicolás Maduro’s regime—ostensibly in the name of stability and economic growth—instead of prioritizing a rapid democratic transition. It appeared to discourage, if not outright block, Machado’s return. That approach simplified the challenge of steering a foreign country, allowing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump to extract what they wanted from Rodríguez. There was no democratic structure to build, no immediate quest for accountability, no need to mediate among competing political factions. The State Department argued that it was supporting incremental reforms that were more likely to stick, and said that a hasty appearance by Machado could cause government institutions and the country’s military to split. But all the while, anger was growing among Venezuelans who had celebrated the removal of Maduro in January. “What Trump has done so far was the easy part,” Steven Levitsky, a professor of Latin American studies at Harvard, told us. “Pushing an authoritarian clique out of power is the hard part. It’s going to take a complex negotiation.”

[From the December 2026 issue: What the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela]

Machado’s return has hastened that negotiation. Last Monday, a senior State Department official told journalists that, as part of the Trump administration’s three-phase plan for Venezuela’s return to democracy, Rodríguez would need to declare a “permanent vacancy in the presidency” once electoral reforms are completed, triggering a six-month period before new elections can occur. This process is highly likely to result in a Machado presidency by mid- to late 2027, at the earliest. Machado’s team has already begun pushing to speed up the pace, knowing that dragging out the process could erode her position.

“Machado is operating on a very tight timeline,” Paul Angelo, a Latin America expert who was previously at the Defense Department and is now at the consultancy McLarty Associates, told us. “She’s the most popular character in the country, but she’s also someone whose cachet as the leader of a unified opposition likely has its limits.”

Neither the United States nor Machado has articulated a postelection plan for Rodríguez and the rest of the Maduro regime should Machado win. There are no easy options: The United States, or another country, could offer them safe haven. Machado could offer them amnesty. Or they could remain in Venezuela, subject to prosecution—the preference of most Machado supporters.

“The ideal is that the Venezuelan courts themselves, the Venezuelan justice system itself, can try and convict those responsible for human-rights abuses,” Martha Tineo, a co-founder of Justicia, Encuentro y Perdón, which tracks forced detentions in Venezuela, told us. “No political agreement of any kind can be above justice.”

The reality is more complicated. If Rodríguez is to remain in power though the elections, potentially standing as a candidate, she will almost certainly want an assurance that she won’t be jailed after the vote. The same is true for much of her regime, including top military and police officials who have committed well-documented human-rights abuses. But the prospect of impunity is abhorrent to Machado’s supporters. Bridging that divide now falls on the United States. Those involved in the democratic transition—reforming and rebuilding Venezuela’s judicial and electoral systems—believe that Washington has the final say over their work. “This whole process originated with a green light from the United States,” one Venezuelan working on the transition told us.

[Read: Why Venezuela?]

Trump’s oil deal could also be complicated by Machado’s return and the restoration of a political opposition in Venezuela. Most of Machado’s supporters believe that the deal is unconstitutional and could be canceled once an independent judiciary is established. (The Trump administration hasn’t released many details about the deal, but has said it was structured to endure over time.) Although Machado had been trying to remain in the White House’s good graces, at her first press conference in Caracas, on Thursday, she said that the agreement “does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants.”

In Rubio’s telling, he cautioned Machado only once against coming back to Venezuela. That was immediately after the devastating June earthquake. At the time, he told reporters last week, the administration was exclusively concerned about ensuring the delivery of aid and feared that her arrival could derail those efforts. That judgment eventually changed. Several weeks ago, Rubio said, the Trump administration warned Rodríguez’s government that Machado had a right to make her widely anticipated return, clearing the way for it to happen. “We spoke to the interim authorities and just said, ‘Look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan; she belongs in her country,’” Rubio said. “She should be allowed to return, and she should be allowed to return unperturbed.”

Rubio has said that the administration will measure Rodríguez’s actions, rather than her rhetoric about its gradual road map for transitioning to an elected government. The map includes plans announced after the most recent round of transition talks among regime figures and a subset of opposition groups, aimed at reforming the country’s highest court and electoral body. Rubio has been open in acknowledging the administration’s willingness to use the threat of reimposing sanctions on Venezuela’s oil sector, or on leaders such as Rodríguez and other senior members of her government, as a coercive tool to avoid foot-dragging.

“No matter what people say along the way, as long as it happens, this is a results-based process,” Rubio said. “So far, frankly, on everything we’ve asked for in this process, be it the economic reforms, the political reforms—it’s happening.”

[Read: Venezuela seems to be going … well?]

Administration officials have voiced periodic frustration with Machado, who they have suggested has at times been impractical and perhaps too willing to compromise stability and economic growth in pursuit of democratic ideals. A State Department spokesperson told us that Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, had been invited to this month’s transition talks in Caracas but did not attend.

Rubio’s plans for Venezuela are nested within a larger Latin America strategy predicated around three interlinked goals: building American commercial primacy by accruing new business deals that squeeze out Chinese firms in the process; defeating drug cartels, using visa sanctions, terror-group designations, and the Pentagon’s militarized partnerships with countries such as Ecuador and Colombia; and choking off illegal migration. Officials see the region’s overall rightward shift as an opportunity to accelerate this approach. Their growing Shield of the Americas initiative is not only a tool for coordinating action against drugs and crime, but also a political counterweight to legacy institutions such as the Organization of American States, which Trump allies see as ineffective and unwilling to act against the region’s leftist strongmen.

Administration officials have pointed to Bolivia, which earlier this year was paralyzed by protests against economic reforms enacted by a conservative government, as a cautionary tale. Bolivia attempted an abrupt change in the midst of an economic crisis, and it backfired for the government. They believe that if Machado had been allowed to take over right after Maduro’s ouster, the same sort of turmoil might have come to Venezuela.

Rubio and other officials have argued that to avoid this kind of outcome, immediate action to revive Venezuela’s economy, particularly in the oil sector, was paramount. Rubio has defended the U.S.-Venezuela oil deal as a practical choice that can ramp up oil output in a way that Chinese and Russian firms never did, and he has downplayed Machado’s criticism of it. But if she becomes the country’s democratically elected president next year, her views will be much more difficult for the Trump administration to ignore.

title: Who Thought This Ad Was a Good Idea?
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.Who says the Midwest is boring? On this election eve, the two most bizarre stories in politics are both...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Who says the Midwest is boring? On this election eve, the two most bizarre stories in politics are both coming out of Senate races in what’s sometimes derided as “flyover country.” But as those of us from the region know, low topography doesn’t mean low drama.

In Michigan, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens—the runner-up in this summer’s primary for a U.S. Senate seat—went literally overnight from grudgingly backing the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed to endorsing the Republican Mike Rogers, as my colleague Jonathan Chait reported. Here we’d customarily explain the reason for her abrupt shift, but Stevens herself couldn’t or wouldn’t articulate that during an excruciating 15-minute interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper. (A follow-up with The Free Press wasn’t clarifying either.)

If El-Sayed loses and Democrats fail to capture a Senate majority, the commotion over Stevens’s flip will appear pivotal. If, however, Republicans lose control of the Senate, then the eye-popping closing ad by Roger Marshall of Kansas, a GOP incumbent, will be a good symbol of where things went wrong for Republicans.

A key issue in the race has been reporting about how Marshall sued more than 700 patients over medical bills. Some paid interest rates as high as 18 percent; 81 arrests were made in relation to medical debt, according to The New York Times. Experts told the paper that such suits are very rare. In an election in which the affordability of basic services is a key issue, these cases have been a millstone around Marshall’s neck, and some polls show him trailing the Democrat Adam Hamilton. Saturday evening, a Kansas City radio host posted a new Marshall ad, featuring the candidate speaking directly to the camera, that apparently aims to turn that around.

“When I practiced as a small-town OB doc, often practicing as the only OB in the middle of 40,000 people, my wife and I decided to take care of everyone, regardless of their ability to pay,” he says. “Now to ensure that 40,000 Kansans would still have access to care, we did have to keep the lights on, so we occasionally handed some accounts over to collection agencies.”

An old political maxim says that “if you’re explaining, you’re losing,” pointing to the importance of not being on the defensive. If that’s true, what does it mean if you’re explaining that you sent hundreds of your constituents to debt collectors over medical bills? The desire to defend oneself against attacks is understandable—though a disciplined candidate doesn’t take bait—but Marshall isn’t even disputing the crux of the attack against him. He’s affirming it. The idea that a candidate would use his final message of the campaign to broadcast these facts to voters is shocking.

His own aides agreed, according to the Times. The paper reported that the senator proposed the ad about two weeks ago, but advisers said it was a bad idea, and that Marshall should “contrast his record with Adam Hamilton, his Democratic rival, especially on immigration.” Instead, Marshall hired a film crew and taped the spot himself, not telling some of his staff. When they found out, they again opposed spending any campaign funds to air it, so Marshall personally started sending it to people outside the campaign. “I would have been glad to put it out much, much sooner,” Marshall told The Wall Street Journal.

Determining what effect it has on the outcome of the race will probably be impossible, but the debacle shows what makes Marshall such a weak candidate. He should be a shoo-in for reelection: He’s a doctor, he’s got a good head of hair, and he’s a Republican in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. When his colleague Jerry Moran ran for reelection, in an underwhelming year for Republicans, he won by 23 percentage points. But Marshall is battling for his career in a race considered a toss-up. The latest Times poll shows Hamilton up 5 percentage points. A Washington Post poll was even more dramatic, showing the Democrat leading by 9 points.

The Kansas race demonstrates some of the reasons this election has been so difficult for the GOP. First, Republicans have some weak candidates. Marshall is not very dynamic, is vulnerable to attacks, and evidently has bad political instincts. Second, Democrats have several unusually strong candidates. Hamilton is a charismatic megachurch pastor. Third, GOP voters—such as the ones who have made Kansas a rock-ribbed Republican state for so long—are unenthusiastic and demotivated. An Emerson College poll found the state’s approval of President Trump underwater, at 45–51, and other polls have similar results. High fuel prices have been a big issue in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state.

Even with all of this, Marshall could win. If he does, it will be a testament to the power of a state’s long record of GOP allegiance to outweigh even an awful campaign. And if he doesn’t win and returns to practicing medicine, prospective patients have been warned about how he handles billing. You can take his word for it.

Today’s News

  1. President Trump asked the Supreme Court to require California to set aside roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots that his administration claims may have been cast by noncitizens. The emergency request followed a federal appeals-court ruling that barred the administration from intervening in California’s ballot-counting procedures.
  2. Iran said that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the United States agrees to lift sanctions and release billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. The announcement came amid renewed negotiations facilitated by Qatari mediators to avert further fighting, though Iran said it was not yet prepared to hold direct talks with U.S. officials.
  3. Democratic Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race yesterday, withdrawing her support for the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated her in the August primary. Stevens said that El-Sayed had excluded her from his campaign, and many Democrats criticized her decision just two days before the election.

Evening Read

Illustration by Alisa Gao / The Atlantic*

The Push to Lead the Working Class Without Workers

By Rose Horowitch

One day over the summer, Morris Katz slouched into our booth at a diner in Brooklyn Heights, removed his backwards baseball cap, and stuffed a Zyn pouch into his mouth. He took out his iPhone (no case, gaping crack down the back) and put it face down on the table. Then, while claiming, “I never do this,” he plunked a Hershey’s Kiss into his espresso. The 27-year-old political strategist and Zohran Mamdani confidant was ready to speak.

Katz believes that the Democratic Party is beholden to billionaire oligarchs and is out of touch with the economic issues that working people care about. The world has worsened for most Americans, and he thinks Democrats are afraid to name the culprits. “You can’t tell someone they’re getting fucked and not tell them who’s fucking them,” Katz said. He loathes politicians who seek incremental change. The party, he says, needs to run outsiders who promise to blow up a corrupt system.

PS

The Senate race in Kansas has one more X factor that’s of special interest to me. Roger Marshall isn’t just facing Adam Hamilton—he’s also being challenged by the libertarian candidate David Graham, who’s drawing 4 percent of the vote in the latest Times/Siena poll, enough to make the difference in a close race. He is not related to me, and I don’t endorse candidates, but I do endorse his name. He should not be confused with David Graham, the Republican nominee for attorney general in Delaware, nor with Mayor David Graham of Princeton, West Virginia, who is not on the ballot this fall. (Neither is any relation to me.) If either candidate wins, they could celebrate with some high-octane honky-tonk from David Graham and the Eskimo Brothers. If things don’t turn out as well for them, I might recommend some slower blues from the late, great British guitarist Davey Graham. They are both—you guessed it—no relation.  

— David

title: The Anger Election’s Final Twist
summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsOver the weekend, in a November surprise, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan primary for U.S. Senate, appeared at Bishop Marvin Winans’s church in Detroit alongside the Republican candidate, Mike ...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Over the weekend, in a November surprise, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan primary for U.S. Senate, appeared at Bishop Marvin Winans’s church in Detroit alongside the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers. She endorsed him soon after, but insisted that she was “not turning my back on Democrats.”

Her endorsement sparked anger among Democrats, who argued that even a vote for Rogers is as good as support for President Trump and his policy agenda—but an endorsement of Rogers is, as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer put it, a “despicable betrayal.”

Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, returned only a small barb as he tried to stay on message: “I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he told a gaggle of reporters. “This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not” Stevens and Rogers.

Many of those voters have been clear about their concerns: They want the government to be less corrupt; they want everyday items to be more affordable; they want an end to the war in Iran. On this week’s episode, my colleagues Gabby Deutch and David A. Graham join me to discuss the issues on voters’ minds as they head into the voting booth, and what the officials they elect can actually do to make them better.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Gabby Deutch: I was just in in Pennsylvania, and I chatted with a couple of college students at East Stroudsburg University, a small school in the Poconos, and they were two guys who had voted for Trump two years ago, and they said, He promised he wouldn’t get us into any more wars, and now our fraternity brother just shipped out to the Middle East. He is in the military and got deployed. And it’s not just about the issues; it’s a sense of feeling lied to.

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and the election is finally here.

The weekend featured a rare November surprise in Michigan, and candidates who’ve been barnstorming their districts and states for months made their final arguments to voters.

My colleagues, Atlantic staff writers Gabby Deutsch and David Graham, joined me to discuss why corruption might be a winning message, how young voters are feeling, and which candidates seem to be delivering actual policy proposals that resonate.

But before we get to questions, I want to remind you that tomorrow, November 3, Radio Atlantic co-host Hanna Rosin and I will be hosting an Election Night livestream starting at 9 p.m.eastern time , where we’ll discuss results and the ideas driving the nation.

All right, let’s get to questions.

Gabby, David—welcome to the show.

David Graham: Thanks for having me.

Deutch: It’s great to be here.

Harris: Gabby, I wanna start with you. We got a rare November surprise over the weekend when Haley Stevens, the Democratic primary challenger to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican Senate candidate, Mike Rogers. Can you just sort of walk us through: What happened there?

Deutch: I think that’s the question that we’re still trying to really find the answer to, in a certain extent. But Haley Stevens lost the Senate primary, of course, to El-Sayed in a pretty close and rather contentious race. It seemed pretty clear over the last few months that they were not the best of friends, to put it mildly, but she did endorse him in the Democratic ticket. Over the last week, things have heated up a bit. There was an ad that came out, not from El-Sayed’s campaign, but promoting him.

Harris: Yeah, let’s talk about that ad for a second. It’s from an outside group, and it tries to tie the high cost of groceries to America’s military support for Israel.

Deutch: And Haley Stevens called on him to condemn that more strongly than he did. He ultimately did distance himself. But through all of it, she said she was still standing by her support for him. And then in the last 48-ish hours, there was a bunch of action on that front. They were going to campaign together, the two of them, at a unity rally in Detroit. And then Haley Stevens put out this statement. El-Sayed said she wasn’t welcome. She was still saying she was endorsing him. And then on Sunday morning, we woke up and saw that Haley Stevens was at church with Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee. I think the question of what exactly changed overnight is still pretty open, and I think all of the campaign reporters in the country are trying to find the answer. But yeah, now we have the loser in the Democratic primary for Senate endorsing the Republican. It’s pretty crazy.

Harris: I guess my question out of that, right—because but you mentioned, right, she’s a loser in the Democratic primary; she’s an outgoing congresswoman at this point. It seemed that Democrats pretty quickly coalesced around, kind of, condemning her endorsement. So does this actually change anything outside of her vote and her support?

Deutch: There is a contingent of some Jewish Democrats and pro-Israel Democrats within Michigan who, since the primary—people who had supported Stevens’s campaign said that they were not going to support El-Sayed. And some in that camp endorsed Rogers. Some said they were going to sit the race out. So that’s been, you know, kind of a small force happening throughout the election. I’m not sure that Stevens making the decision to endorse Rogers really grows it. It’s already been building, kind of, organically in a section of the Jewish community that’s unhappy with El-Sayed’s language about Israel and Zionism and some Jewish-aligned issues. But, you know, I think we’ve seen from the Rogers campaign—they’re obviously very excited about this and hoping that if there are people who are still on the fence at this point. And El-Sayed and Rogers are pulling—El-Sayed seems to be in the lead, but it’s closer than in the governor’s race in Michigan as well. So if there were holdouts who were looking for a sign, I think maybe, you know, for that handful of people who could be relevant—or who could be decisive—that is, you know, they think perhaps this is the thing that does it.

Harris: Yeah. David—El-Sayed said:

Abdul El-Sayed: At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens. See what I’m saying? I think about the, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am the policy of it all.

Harris: And there are several big issues, right, driving the voters to the polls in this election, right? Affordability, economy, health care, war in Iran. But you also recently wrote about how corruption is weighing on voters’ minds in this election cycle. What are the polls telling us about what voters are thinking about?

Graham: Yeah, I was just really struck looking at some of the late polling, just in the last couple weeks, sort of mid-to-late October. Several polls from Fox News, from the Financial Times, from CNBC, all found corruption topping voters’ list of issues. And that’s striking because we’ve seen so much focus on affordability, and I think rightly so. It is kind of a truism of, you know, data-informed political reporting that money issues are what moves votes. And here we have a case where corruption, which is not purely a money issue, is at the top of lists.

To me I think what we see is—surprisingly, given the party’s, kind of, chaos, including in that Michigan race—a, kind of, success of Democratic messaging where they’ve managed to put together the kind of democratic, you know, pro-democracy concerns that some people thought were a political loser and these economic concerns into a package and be like, What this election is about is corruption. And I think that’s a way for them to attack Republicans across the board.

Harris: Yeah. Gabby, you’ve been on the ground talking to voters in Pennsylvania and Ohio, and you’re heading to Michigan today to cover Election Day. What are you hearing from voters in those states?

Deutch: I think corruption, actually, to David’s point, is a huge issue. And it’s a little surprising because Democrats have been talking for years about, right, the threats to democracy from Trump, oligarchy, corruption, but it hasn’t quite gotten through. But now when the prices of everything is so high, that message lands in a different way. And so I think that’s consistent for any Democrat who’s doing well right now, and I mean, and talking to voters as well—I was just in Pennsylvania, and I chatted with a couple of college students at a at East Stroudsburg University, a small school in the Poconos, and they were two guys who had voted for Trump two years ago, and they said, He promised he wouldn’t get us into any more wars, and now our fraternity brother just shipped out to the Middle East. He is in the military and got deployed. And it’s not just about the issues; it’s a sense of feeling lied to. And I think there’s a lot of that right now, and Democrats are trying to tap into that anger.

Harris: Yeah. David, kind of to that point, right? It’s the ability to put one to one, right? You said you weren’t going to start a foreign war. Now my fraternity brother is being sent overseas. You said that you were going to lower the price of these everyday items. And we’ve heard about this thing that’s happening in Iran, and now my gas is more expensive. How much does—

Graham: You said you would release the Epstein files, and now it looks like you’re covering them up—which is another, sort of a different, form of corruption, but I think it matches in there too. Yeah.

Harris: Yeah. So Gabby, you know, thinking about those young folks in Pennsylvania—you mentioned that these were Trump supporters. Is this a broader thing, or does it seem as if this is a broader thing?

Deutch: I think these couple of voters that I spoke to are certainly indicative of some larger trends we’re seeing, which is namely that among a lot of the youngest voters—you know, these are people who are 21 and 22. There’s not really a sense of party loyalty, at least not yet. And, you know, I think a decade or so ago, the conventional wisdom was that young voters were pretty liberal. But then a couple years ago, we saw a big swing among younger voters towards Trump. I think what we’re seeing in this election—and there’s, you know, polling and research that indicates this as well—is that young voters are very much up for grabs and they want to feel like they’re voting for a leader who is not going to lie to them, for example, and not going to say, I’m gonna stay out of wars, and then start a war in Iran. So I would call young voters very much a swing group, and I think a lot of campaigns are recognizing that.

Harris: The thing that I’ve been wondering is people sort of call this the “anger election,” but anger only, sort of, lasts so long. I guess, is this something that Democrats see as sustainable for not just maybe 2026, but on towards 2028?

Graham: Well, I think there’s a question of campaign, and there’s a question of governing. Corruption is a really good message for people. And you know, I think voters are always upset about corruption. They tend to think the government is corrupt. Maybe we’re reaching a kind of tipping point, because some of the instances that we have seen have been so brazen—you know, hidden donations to a White House ballroom and so on and so forth. So maybe there is a tipping point.

But the problem is really what happens when you get in government. Because you see voters of both parties who are upset about this. But we see a, kind of, hamstrung government. Let’s say Democrats ride this messaging to a win in the House and the Senate. What are they going to do once they’re in? Okay, they can launch a lot of investigations, which will uncover more corruption. They can maybe even impeach some Cabinet members. We’ll see. But, you know, it’s an open question how much difference they can make when they do not—you know, they only have control of one or two houses of Congress. And I think this gets to the general sort of “calcification,” as political scientists call it, of electoral politics and of policy. When no party has a clear majority or could win an outright majority because things are so closely divided, it’s hard to really have lasting policy change. And I think that’s one reason voters are frustrated and voters are disillusioned, and so many voters say the country is on the wrong path.

Harris: Gabby, when you’re talking to people, are there things that they say, you know, actively might excite them? Are there, sort of, affirmative visions for what they would be willing to vote for outside of what they’re willing to vote against?

Deutch: I think for a lot of the voters that I spoke with, it’s pretty simple what they want. Government actually doing it is another question. They want lower prices. A lot of people want to see an end to the war with Iran. Even for supporters of the war with Iran who, let’s say, want to see the Iranian regime taken down—that, as we’ve now seen from several months of this, that’s not an easy thing to do. And so when I was in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, you know, would give this stump speech, and he spoke pretty straightforwardly. When I’m elected, I’m going to end the Iran war, end the tariffs, and lower gas prices. And those are three great things to say. To do those things and actually make sure that they come with, you know, a decrease in the cost of living to change the quality-of-life concerns that voters have is obviously a lot harder. And I think a lot of this is, you know, Let’s try to ride this, this wave of anger, and once we get to Washington, we’ll figure it out.

Graham: I’ve been seeing a similar thing in North Carolina, where we have a Senate race and Roy Cooper, the Democrat, is expected to win very comfortably. And Cooper’s been out on this “make stuff cost less” tour. That’s kind of his headline approach for campaigning. And you know, he spent eight years as a popular governor and I think is used to being able to do things, but as one senator, maybe in the majority and maybe not, I don’t know how much impact he’s going to be able to have. And so I wonder about the, you know, about the wisdom or about the value of these kinds of promises.

Deutch: Well, I just said one thing, which is—and I don’t know the likelihood of this actually coming to fruition, but I have seen a lot of, among particularly some congressional swing seats in Pennsylvania where the Democratic candidates are talking about ending stock trading among members of Congress. That’s something that, to the corruption point, seems to be coming up a lot and perhaps resonating more with voters this year: this idea that—and this is directly what I heard some candidates say—that members of Congress are learning information, let’s say, about the war, and then they’re able to trade stocks in defense companies and get rich off of your sorrow as Americans. So I think we’ll see more of a push on that front. I don’t know how likely that actually will be to happen.

Harris: Are there any other candidates who might have laid out other policies, right? So thinking about corruption, are there candidates who’ve laid out policy visions that actually seem, right, practical? Because like you said, David, for the next two years, if Democrats do win power in the House, they’ll have investigatory power over, you know, different members of the Cabinet, members of the administration. But for two years it’s going to be, it would be a lame-duck session, right? So there wouldn’t be a lot of legislating happening. But are there, sort of, policy ideas being laid out to address those other concerns that voters have that seem that they could be in a reasonable timeline?

Graham: Well you know, Trump was saying in the last few days that if Democrats win Congress, he will become Mr. Veto, which seems like he’s right about that. I think Gabby’s example of the stock-trading ban is a really interesting one, because that’s the kind of thing that you could imagine actually winning bipartisan support. In fact, we’ve seen versions of this law that are just not really, don’t have teeth, attempted. That’s a bipartisan enough thing; you could imagine Republicans backing it and Trump having to then either sign it or veto it. But it’s hard to think of other things. For example, you know, if we talk about health care; if we talk about—you know, it’s hard to imagine what Republicans and Democrats would agree on. It’s hard to imagine Democrats forcing an end to the war. It’s just the things that they have power over from Congress, I think, are fairly limited.

Deutch: I think we’ll see, if Democrats take power in the House and/or the Senate, some efforts to try to reverse some of the changes and cuts that were made by the Trump administration to Medicare and Medicaid and health care more broadly. That’s challenging when there is legislation that was passed by Congress that Trump signed implementing some of those cuts. But I would imagine there will be, you know, ways to look at that and make sure some people keep health-care coverage who were going to lose it. But that’s not something that’s going to be easy for Democrats, certainly.

Harris: When we return, Gabby and David tell me the races they’ll be following most closely on Election Night.

[Break]

Harris: So the president rallied in Kansas and Iowa over the weekend. He’s expected to speak Monday at the Reflecting Pool in Washington to make a closing pitch to voters.

Graham: It’s fascinating to make your closing pitch in front of a huge symbol of incompetence during your administration.

Harris: Yeah, you know, and David, I was gonna say—because we spoke about this back in July, right? That, you know, given the ways that this venue, sort of, exemplifies, highlights that disconnect between the president’s, the things that he values, right? The appearance of the nation’s capital and building the archway and, you know, the Reflecting Pool and the things that voters say that they care about, which is like trying to get to work and it’s way more expensive than it used to be. What does that exemplify about that misalignment between the president and the voters? And is there any way that he’s trying to close that gap in this last couple of days?

Graham: Yeah, I mean I obviously don’t know what’s going to happen in the election, but to the extent that Republicans are on the defensive, I think Trump’s handling of the last few days of the campaign show that. Having a rally at the Reflection Pool does that. These rallies in Kansas and Iowa do that too. The White House announced they were canceling these rallies. And then Trump seems to have been basically goaded into putting them back on the schedule because a reporter for Reuters asked him if he was sick or if he wasn’t feeling well and why he was canceling them. And he seems to have reacted to that with a, like, Okay, well then, I’ll just go ahead and do it, although not without sort of tasteless remarks about the reporter’s physique. And that lack of discipline or a guiding principle or sort of interest in what voters actually care about, I think is why Republicans are in a difficult spot and why, you know, the president has become something of an albatross for many of them.

Harris: So tomorrow is Election Night. What will you both be watching for, right? Are there races that you’ll be paying attention to that could be sort of bellwethers for the rest of the night? And Gabby, I’ll start with you.

Deutch: Sure, I’ll talk a little bit again about Pennsylvania. Just something that I found very interesting on my trip there last week is that Josh Shapiro, who’s running for reelection, and polling shows him ahead of his Republican opponent 25 points, which is sort of—I mean, he’s very popular, but it’s still pretty shocking in a state that Trump won two years ago. He’s hardly even campaigning for reelection. Really, what he’s doing is, kind of, this tour around the state promoting state and local candidates, and also four Democrats running in swing congressional seats. And he wants to be able to say, I flipped Congress, to say, I gave Democrats this check on Trump. And those, I think, four seats are places that I’ll be watching.

Paige Cognetti, for example, the mayor of Scranton, who’s running against a congressman named Rob Bresnahan, or Janelle Stelson, who is running against Scott Perry, who is a prominent supporter of election deniers and promoting election-related conspiracy theories. So those are a couple of the races that I’ll be watching.

And then in Michigan, where I’ll be spending Election Day and Night and some time this week, just how much of, as we’ve spoken about, of an impact Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers has and looking at the difference between how El-Sayed does and Jocelyn Benson, who’s a Democrat running for governor, who is polling a lot better than El-Sayed. And so is she and,kind of, the general anger at Republicans going to be able to pull El-Sayed over the finish line, despite some of these interruptions that he probably rather would not have dealt with in the closing days?

Harris: Yeah. David, same question to you.

Graham: I guess a couple of races I’ll be looking for just as indicators are the New Hampshire Senate race and the South Carolina Senate race. And so in both of those cases—in New Hampshire we expect Democrat Chris Pappas to win. In South Carolina we expect Republican Darline Graham to win. But how close those races are, I think, will be a useful indicator. If John Sununu keeps that close in New Hampshire, I think it’s not gonna be an overwhelming night for Democrats. If, on the other hand, Annie Andrews is very close to Darline Graham in South Carolina, that’s a sign that Republicans are going to be on the ropes for the rest of the evening. And so those might be early signs. But I mean, the other thing that I am really desperately trying to do is not to overreact to early results. I have been thinking back to the 2018 election, when, on Election Night, a lot of commentators declared that there was no blue wave and that it had been a real underwhelming night for Democrats. And then after a lot of races that were close or hadn’t been counted yet came in, it turned out to be a pretty good night for Democrats. So I just, I’m trying to remind myself that we really don’t know on Election Night. There’ll be a lot of races we can’t tell, and I’m going to try to hold my analysis until I have a better sense of the whole picture.

Deutch: I was just going to follow David and say that his reminder is the most important one and we all like to spend our evenings on Election Day on Twitter and calling people as soon as the polls close. And at that point, no one knows anything, including all the people that we’re calling. It’s always a good reminder to ourselves as journalists to not be drawing those conclusions too early.

Harris: Yeah, absolutely. Well, David, Gabby, thank you so much for joining me and helping us better understand what to pay attention to; what, maybe, to give a little less credence to; and also, we’ll be following your reporting as Election Day moves on and into the next couple of weeks. So thank you so much for joining.

Deutsch: Thank you.

Graham: Thank you.

Harris: That’s all for today’s show. Don’t forget, this Tuesday night, November 3, we’re going to host a special Election Night livestream. I’ll be joined by my Radio Atlantic co-host, Hanna Rosin, where we’ll be talking with Atlantic staff writers like Tom Nichols, Mark Leibovich, and Tyler Austin Harper, among others, about the midterm results as they come in and their theories about where the nation could be headed. We’ll be live for two hours starting at 9 p.m. eastern.

This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

content:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job

content:
Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

content:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
summary: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatmentThe “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials....
content:
Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’

content:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
